masthead_title: A hot inflation report just pushed the Fed toward a bigger December rate hike — but only bonds and chip stocks felt it today.
regime_line: October's inflation report ran hot — core prices up 0.3% against a 0.2% forecast, headline up 0.4% against 0.3% — and bond traders moved fast: the 2-year Treasury yield jumped 17 basis points to 4.73%, and the odds of a December Fed rate hike rose to roughly 90%, from about 72% a week ago. The 30-year Treasury's 5.35% close sits at a level this market held routinely before 2002, with only a brief echo in 2007 since (today's lead History fact, below). Stocks barely noticed outside of chips: the S&P 500 fell just 0.38% while the already-weak semiconductor sector (Tier 3, below) did the real damage.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — two resolved, four still open

Every open conditional claim (§4B) is checked against Tuesday's close and today's CPI print before any new narrative is written.

  • CL-0065 (front-end repricing vs. CPI, due today) — confirmed. October Core CPI printed +0.3% m/m (at the test's confirm bar, above the 0.2% consensus) and the 2-year Treasury closed at 4.73% Tuesday, well above Friday's 4.51% confirm line. Fed-hike odds for December moved to roughly 88–90% (from about 72% a week earlier), with Governor Waller floating a possible 50bp move — a durable hawkish repricing, not a one-day reaction.
  • CL-0059 (Gartner, due today) — expired, unresolved. The five-session window (Nov. 4–10, with today as the deadline check) is complete. Gartner broke the "every session at or below $204.22" confirm path on day one ($207.19 Nov. 4) but never approached the $220 refute line (window high was that same $207.19); it then drifted lower every session, closing $188.92 Tuesday. Neither durable skepticism nor a clean overreaction on the letter of the test — it just kept sliding past where either line would have told us something.
  • CL-0060 (Vistra, due 2026-11-12): four of five sessions in, confirm path already broken (day two's $124.80 close was above the $120.29 base) but the $135 refute line still untouched — window high remains Monday's $133.92; Vistra pulled back to $131.18 Tuesday, $3.82 short of refute.
  • CL-0061 (FIS, due 2026-11-12): four of five sessions in, confirm path intact — FIS closed $28.31 Tuesday, still at or below its $29.76 base on every session so far; not a refute (needs $34).
  • CL-0064 (stock/credit divergence, due 2026-11-16): two of five sessions in — neither side has won. The S&P 500 closed $7,520.93 Tuesday, still above both the Thursday ($7,353.73) and Friday ($7,376.86) reference closes equities would need to hold or break; credit (dated Monday, 11-09) hasn't eased below |z| 1.5 either, though it keeps moving that direction.
  • CL-0066 (credit stabilizing vs. confirming, due 2026-11-13): one of three sessions in — both HY OAS (z +2.04, was +2.46) and IG OAS (z +2.19, was +2.68) eased further today, neither back below the |z| 1.5 line yet, and neither rose above its prior reading either. Still tracking toward stabilization, not there yet.
story_html:
Today's coverage (Yahoo Finance, CNBC, Kiplinger, Investing.com) centers on one number: October Core CPI rose 0.3% month-over-month, above the 0.2% consensus, with headline CPI up 0.4% against a 0.3% forecast — the third straight month core inflation has run at 0.3% (Investing.com attributed some of the heat to high energy costs and AI-buildout-related pricing). Treasury yields jumped on the print, led by the front end: the 2-year rose 17bp to 4.73%. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he's “leaning toward” a December hike and that a 50-basis-point move “should be considered” if inflation keeps running hot (CNBC); CME FedWatch odds for a December hike jumped to roughly 88–90% (Investing.com), up from about 72% a week ago. Stocks opened lower and stayed there, with the Nasdaq Composite down about 0.8% at the open as Nvidia weighed on tech (Yahoo Finance).

This system's own pull backs the yield move and adds two pieces this morning's headlines didn't dwell on. First, credit kept improving rather than confirming the rate scare: HY OAS (the extra yield lenders demand to hold junk-rated debt, dated Monday 11-09 on its usual one-day lag) eased another 8bp to 3.34% (z +2.04, still flagged but down from Monday's +2.46), and IG OAS eased 2bp to 0.91% (z +2.19, down from +2.68) — the second straight session of easing, the live CL-0066 test (Flags, below). Second, the equity reaction was narrow, not broad: the S&P 500 fell 0.38% to 7,520.93 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.74%, but the equal-weight S&P (RSP) barely moved, down just 0.03% — today's concept, below. The damage concentrated in chips: the semiconductor ETF SMH fell another 0.78% to a fresh multi-week low (z −2.48, this run's largest single-series flag, Chart of the day), with Nvidia's 5.47% drop doing most of the work. The dollar firmed on the hawkish repricing, DXY up 0.57% to 102.23 (z +1.53, newly re-flagged).

Two of today's three qualifying movers were earnings- or guidance-driven and moved against the broader tape's weakness; the third, Nvidia, sits at the center of today's one concentrated pullback (Movers, below).
dashboard_interp_html:
The front end of the curve did almost all of today's work, and it just got the clearest possible reason to move. The 3-month bill rose 6bp to 4.30% (z +1.81, flagged; 53rd percentile since 1977 but the 71st of the last 30 years, no real gap). The 2-year, the part of the curve that functions as a running poll of Fed expectations, rose 17bp to 4.73% (z +1.29, not flagged; 52nd percentile since 1977 but the 81st of the last 30 years, † — cite both, a 30-point gap). The 10-year rose 10bp to 4.98% (z +0.83; 46th/83rd, †) and the 30-year rose 9bp to 5.35% (z +0.69; 47th/82nd, † — today's lead History-check fact, below, where that gap matters even more). Why this matters: when the front end jumps on a data print like this, it's repricing how many more times (and how soon) the Fed hikes, not the growth or inflation outlook for the next decade — closer to what moves a new CD rate or a variable-rate loan than a 30-year mortgage quote, though today's move was broad enough up the curve to touch mortgage quotes too.

The curve itself flattened on that front-end-led move: 2s10s fell 7bp to 25bp (28th/29th percentile, no real gap, nowhere near inversion), while 3m10y actually widened 4bp to 68bp — the belly of the curve, not the very front, absorbed most of today's move.

Credit went the other way, which is the day's real tension. HY OAS (dated Monday 11-09, the usual one-day lag) eased 8bp to 3.34% (z +2.04, still flagged; 81st percentile of its own ~3-year record, §4F, marked *). IG OAS (also dated 11-09) eased 2bp to 0.91% (z +2.19, still flagged; 66th percentile of its own ~3-year record, also *). SOFR (also dated 11-09) eased 1bp to 3.88% (z +1.34, not flagged; 45th percentile since 1954 but the 67th of the last 30 years, †, a 22-point gap). Why this matters: lenders aren't demanding more compensation for risk today, even as the Fed-path repricing makes new borrowing itself more expensive — two different dials (Unit 3), both worth watching on their own terms.

The dollar firmed on the hawkish repricing, DXY up 0.57% to 102.23 (newly re-flagged, z +1.53; 72nd/81st percentile, no real gap). Fed balance-sheet and TGA readings are still last Wednesday's H.4.1/DTS release, carried forward unchanged — both structurally modern-only instruments (no pre-2008 "normal" exists to compare against, §4F, so none is offered). ON RRP ticked down to $0.15B (z −0.52, not flagged; also modern-only). Why this matters: a firmer dollar on a day the Fed looks set to hike again raises the cost of dollar debt and dollar-priced commodities for the rest of the world — the carry-and-transmission loop Unit 5 covered.
history_html:
Today's deepest echo is still the 30-year Treasury, up 9bp to 5.35% — held on 26 of the last 43 sessions since first reaching it Sep. 10; before this run, last seen briefly in June 2007 (one session), and routinely only until February 2002. The split matters: today's level beats 82 of every 100 days of the last 30 years but just the 47th percentile since 1977, a 35-point gap (†), because the full record folds in the double-digit yields of the early 1980s, every one of which sat above today's 5.35%. “Elevated against the last 30 years, unremarkable against the full record” is the honest read, not a downgrade.

The then-vs-now panel pairs today against June 2007. The 10-year lines up closely (4.98% now vs. 5.26% then) and the curve shape is similar (2s10s 25bp now vs. 18bp then). What doesn't: SOFR today (3.88%) sits well below the Fed funds rate then (5.26%), and the direction is opposite — the Fed back then was headed toward cuts, while today's repricing (CL-0065, confirmed this morning) points toward another hike.

Second fact: the 10-year TIPS real yield (2.66%, Monday's print) sits at the 99th percentile of its own 23-year record. TIPS only exist since 2003, though; the Cleveland Fed's model real rate, back to 1982, puts the same concept at a milder 80th percentile of the last 30 years, just the 54th since 1982 — two stories, one number.

Third: the 2-year's 126bp rise this year is the 9th-largest through this date in 50 years, tied with 1987. Client-ready line: the 30-year's level has been seen before, just not recently, under a looser Fed; the 2-year's speed — top-10 out of 50 years — is the part that's actually unusual.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically, plus the top-50 megacaps; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) or a sector ETF diverging ≥1.5pp from SPX, never by seeming interesting. 19 name candidates and 0 sector divergences qualified Tuesday — no sector note today, and the cap holds at 3 names.

Charter Communications +10.61% (134.06, from 121.20) — what happened: the day's largest percentage gainer, recovering more than half of last Friday's post-earnings drop. Stated reason: Wells Fargo raised its price target on Charter to $103 from $101 Tuesday (kept an Underweight rating) (MarketBeat); the stock has been rebuilding since Friday's Q3 report, which showed a $6.3bn franchise-impairment charge and continued pro forma internet-subscriber losses but also management's new $2bn cost-savings target (RTTNews, 247wallst). Read-through: idiosyncratic — a single analyst price-target change and a post-earnings bounce in a company-specific broadband-subscriber story, not a consumer-spending signal.

Take-Two Interactive +8.31% (224.64, from 207.40) — what happened: one of the day's largest megacap-adjacent gainers, moving against the broader tape's weakness. Stated reason: CEO Strauss Zelnick said pre-orders for Grand Theft Auto VI (out Nov. 19) are tracking "far in excess" of the company's initial expectations (Yahoo Finance), even as the quarter's own bookings missed Take-Two's guided range and revenue came in roughly in line ($1.601bn vs. $1.607bn consensus). Read-through: idiosyncratic — a single-title demand signal ahead of the industry's most-anticipated release this year, not a broader consumer-spending read.

Nvidia −5.47% (168.89, from 178.67) — what happened: the day's largest megacap decliner, and the single biggest driver of the SMH weakness behind today's chart of the day. Stated reason: part of the day's broader hot-CPI-driven tech selloff (Yahoo Finance's Tuesday live coverage specifically named Nvidia among the names weighing on tech), compounding the still-unresolved board investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's conduct first reported this past weekend (Associated Press, ABC News). Read-through: mixed — mostly idiosyncratic (the governance overhang is company-specific), but layered on top of a real macro input today (the rate-driven tech pullback); no fresh negative signal on AI-chip demand itself surfaced today, unlike the governance story.
chart_of_day_why: SMH is this run's largest Tier 1/Tier 3 |z| flag (−2.48), the clearest single series behind today's semis-led decline — Nvidia's 5.47% drop (Movers, above) did most of the work, pushing the semiconductor ETF's level to a fresh multi-week low relative to its own trailing six months, even as the broader market's reaction to today's hot CPI print stayed narrow (Story and Concept, above and below).
tier3_html:
Daily read: SMH underperformed SPY by about 0.4 percentage points Tuesday (−0.78% vs. −0.37%), a smaller gap than some recent sessions but the same direction — the chip/AI-hardware complex still the softest corner of the market three weeks after the early-November selloff began. Nvidia's governance overhang (Movers, above) is doing most of the work today; no fresh demand-side news, positive or negative, surfaced for the sector.

Weekly issuance/spread note: no fresh, dated hyperscaler-issuance or vendor-financing news surfaced in today's search. This morning's HY/IG OAS prints, dated Monday 11-09 (Dashboard, above), both still flagged but easing for a second straight session, remain the live reading on financing-side risk appetite. The next structured Tier 3 half-page runs Friday (§5).
calendar_note_html:
Today: a quiet calendar by design — today is Veterans Day, a SIFMA-recommended bond-market holiday (no Treasury cash trading, so no fresh Treasury/OAS/SOFR fill is expected for today's date). Equities remain open and trading normally. This week's calendar cache shows no other scheduled high-impact release today.

Why this matters to the current regime: with no fresh data due today, the question is whether yesterday's hawkish repricing (CL-0065, confirmed this morning) holds into next week without a new catalyst to test it — which is exactly what the new CL-0067 claim (Flags, below) is built to check. A quiet calendar day is also a fair test of whether today's narrow, chips-only equity reaction (Concept, below) broadens out once the CPI print is a day old, or stays contained.
concept_title: When the hierarchy splits three ways, not two — rates, credit, and breadth can each be right about a different question
concept_html: Segments 1-4 built the hierarchy habit on a two-way split: rates against credit, or stocks against credit. Today splits three ways, and each piece is actually answering a different question. Rates and the dollar answered the policy question, cleanly: a hot CPI print pushed the 2-year yield up 17bp and December hike odds to roughly 90% — a real, data-confirmed repricing (CL-0065), not noise. Credit answered the risk question, and gave the opposite-sounding signal: HY and IG OAS both kept easing today (z +2.04 and +2.19, down from +2.46 and +2.68), a second straight session of improvement, not deterioration. Equity breadth answered a third question entirely — how widely is this being felt — and the answer is narrow: the S&P 500 fell 0.38% but the equal-weight average barely moved, down just 0.03%, meaning the selling sat almost entirely in one sector (chips, Tier 3 above) rather than across the market. None of these three actually contradicts the others once you ask what each one is measuring: more Fed hikes are coming (rates), lenders aren't newly worried about defaults (credit), and today's selling was concentrated, not systemic (breadth). The hierarchy habit isn't about picking a winner among three readings — it's matching each one to the question it's actually equipped to answer.
client_translation: Rates moved today because the Fed is more likely to hike again in December — that's a different thing from markets getting nervous about defaults or a broad selloff, and today's data shows neither of those happening.
client_lens_html:
“Is the Fed raising rates again?” Today's hotter-than-expected inflation report pushed the market's odds of a December hike to around 90%, from about 72% a week ago. If that holds, it argues for things tied to short rates — new CD yields, money-market rates, credit-card APRs — staying higher for longer, even if a 30-year mortgage quote (tied more to the long end) doesn't move as much.

“Why did Nvidia drop again?” Today's drop was partly the broader market's reaction to the inflation report (tech led the selling) and partly the still-unresolved board investigation into the CEO's conduct — two separate things stacking on the same stock. Neither one is new information about whether companies are still buying AI chips.

“The market barely moved today, right?” The headline S&P 500 number (down 0.38%) undersells how narrow today's decline was — the average stock, measured without letting the giant tech names dominate, was basically flat. Two of today's three biggest movers (Charter, Take-Two) were actually up sharply on their own company news. Worth remembering before assuming a down headline day means a bad day for every account.
